Node states 'Mininet fork (Containernet) that runs Docker containers as emulated hosts with runtime add/remove' — extends Mininet for NFV/MEC/fog service prototyping.
Node states it 'Extends Mininet with virtual Wi-Fi stations and access points plus propagation and mobility models' — the SDN-wireless extension of Mininet.
Node states it 'Distributes Mininet across a cluster of workers via GRE tunnels and a configurable time-dilation factor' — scales the Mininet emulator to thousands of nodes.
Mininet-HiFi adds container-based CPU/bandwidth resource isolation and a fidelity monitor to Mininet, making its emulated experiments performance-faithful and reproducible.
Emulab established the integrated real-node emulation testbed with time/space multiplexing; Mininet miniaturizes that emulation model onto a single laptop, so Emulab's testbed concepts underpin it.
Mininet's software switches (Open vSwitch) speak OpenFlow, so the emulator instantiates OpenFlow-based SDN prototyping — its founding purpose.
CrystalNet is the later cloud-scale, high-fidelity descendant of Emulab's run-real-code testbed idea, booting production device firmware images loaded with real configs.
The CORE manual/model documentation and the introducing paper 'CORE: A Real-Time Network Emulator' describe the same tool — sibling artifacts of one effort, no precedence.
CORE and Mininet are parallel OS-namespace emulators; CORE emphasizes real-time operation, wireless/mobility scripting and hardware-in-the-loop, Mininet targets SDN/OpenFlow prototyping.
Kathara and containerlab are the two main declarative, container-based network-lab emulators, wiring Docker/generic containers into reproducible YAML topologies for labs and CI.
containerlab and Containernet both emulate network services from containers — containerlab wires vendor NOS/Linux containers via YAML, Containernet runs Docker hosts inside Mininet.
Kollaps (decentralized, tc/eBPF, no central emulator) and MaxiNet (GRE-tunneled cluster distribution) are parallel approaches to scaling container/SDN emulation across many machines.
Both use time dilation / virtual time to decouple emulation from wall-clock and overcome host resource limits — MaxiNet's configurable time-dilation factor and TimeKeeper's kernel virtual clock.
TimeKeeper's controllable virtual time for real emulation parallels Shadow's simulated-time discrete-event execution of real applications — both make experiments independent of wall-clock speed.
Both emulate end-to-end path properties (delay/bandwidth/loss) for unmodified applications — Kollaps via tc/eBPF topology shaping, Mahimahi via record-and-replay link shells.
Kernel virtual time is the enabling mechanism for the timing fidelity that container-based faithful emulation (Mininet-HiFi) strives to guarantee under host resource contention.
Mininet (emulation of real code in namespaces) and ns-3 (discrete-event simulation) are the two dominant open network-experimentation platforms, chosen by the fidelity/scale trade-off.
Mininet emulation versus OMNeT++ component-based discrete-event simulation — parallel paradigms for network-protocol experimentation.
Container-based reproducible emulation experiments and the simulation-credibility critique are parallel efforts to make network-experiment results trustworthy and repeatable.
Pantheon builds its calibrated emulated network paths using Mahimahi's link/delay/loss emulation shells as the record-and-replay engine.
Adds a lightweight virtual switch to raise P4-emulation fidelity and throughput beyond the BMv2 reference software switch, the standard but slow P4 dataplane target.
BMv2 is the reference behavioral-model implementation of the P4 abstract switch, executing compiled P4 programs.
Titled 'A Survey on Data Plane Programming with P4: Fundamentals, Advances, and...' — it catalogs the P4 language work and its ecosystem.
The comprehensive SDN survey extensively catalogs OpenFlow, the protocol that launched software-defined networking, as the field's foundational enabling work.
The SDN survey cites Mininet as the de-facto SDN prototyping and emulation environment for experimenting with OpenFlow controllers.
P4sim brings the P4 programmable-data-plane model into ns-3, instantiating P4 packet processing inside the simulator.
Mininet-WiFi (software Wi-Fi/propagation-model emulation) and Colosseum (large-scale hardware RF channel emulator) are wireless-network emulators at opposite fidelity/scale points.
GARNET is a component of gem5: "A Detailed On-Chip Network Model Inside a Full-System Simulator ... now gem5's Ruby" on-chip network model.
"The macroscale (SST/macro) element of Sandia's Structural Simulation Toolkit" — SST/macro is a module of SST.
ROSS is an optimistic "Time Warp" engine; the Time Warp / optimistic-synchronization mechanism originates in Jefferson's Virtual Time.
Reverse computation is "the defining method behind ROSS" for memory-frugal rollback instead of state-saving.
CODES torus/dragonfly models are "running on ROSS" — CODES instantiates the ROSS Time Warp engine.
Reverse computation refines Time Warp's rollback, replacing state-saving with invertible event handlers; later work in Jefferson's optimistic lineage.
WARPED is a configurable Time Warp kernel implementing Jefferson's optimistic Virtual Time mechanism (antimessages, GVT).
muSik's optimistic mode uses Time Warp state-saving synchronization derived from Virtual Time (it also supports conservative).
Warp Speed is a strong-scaling benchmark of ROSS (PHOLD at ~504B events/s) on ~2M Blue Gene/Q cores.
The 2M-core study runs "ROSS Time Warp + reverse computation" — it applies the reverse-computation rollback method.
Ramulator is the faster (~2.5x), template-based, more extensible DRAM simulator that largely displaced DRAMSim2 for new memory studies.
DiskSim (storage subsystem) and DRAMSim2 (memory subsystem) are sibling device-level timing simulators that add detailed subsystem fidelity to full-system studies.
SST's memHierarchy can drive DRAMSim2 as its DRAM-timing backend, using its cycle-accurate memory engine as a component model.
gem5 integrates Ramulator (via its gem5 wrapper) as an external cycle-level DRAM model.
BookSim (standalone) and GARNET (embedded in full-system simulators) are the two canonical cycle-accurate interconnection/NoC simulators.
ASTRA-SIM drives gem5's Garnet as a cycle-accurate network backend to model collective communication over the fabric.
GTNetS and PDNS are both Georgia Tech (Riley/Fujimoto) MPI-parallel packet-level network simulators scaling to hundreds of thousands of elements.
Both concern conservative (null-message) synchronization for parallel large-scale packet-level network simulation.
SimGrid (SMPI) and SST/macro both coarsely simulate skeletonized HPC/MPI applications over modeled network platforms.
muSik and WARPED are both reusable/configurable PDES kernels serving as testbeds for synchronization-algorithm research.
SimAI's distributed-DL-training infrastructure simulator builds on and references the ASTRA-SIM co-design approach.
The PDES survey catalogs optimistic synchronization / the Time Warp mechanism originating in Virtual Time.
The PDES survey catalogs conservative synchronization algorithms for large-scale simulation.
Two index entries for the ASTRA-SIM distributed-DL-training simulator.
Fujimoto's book "Parallel and Distributed Simulation Systems" consolidates and generalizes his CACM "Parallel Discrete Event Simulation" survey.
ns-3's architecture and scalability lineage trace to Riley's GTNetS (shared author and design ancestry).
CODES/ROSS (dragonfly/torus, optimistic) and SST/macro (coarse-grained) are parallel large-scale HPC-interconnect PDES models — bridging the PDES-engine and architecture-simulator lineages.

CloudSim Plus is a ground-up modular re-engineering of the CloudSim codebase (now Java 17+); its own summary calls it a re-engineering that 'effectively supersedes' CloudSim as the maintained implementation most new projects adopt.

iFogSim is 'built on CloudSim' (endpoint description), reusing CloudSim's discrete-event engine and datacenter/VM/host abstractions to model cloud-fog-IoT hierarchies and placement/offloading policies.
iFogSim2's description states it 'Extends and supersedes iFogSim', adding real EUA mobility traces, dynamic distributed clustering and microservice orchestration.
iFogSim2, like its predecessor, still runs on the CloudSim engine, inheriting its discrete-event core and datacenter abstractions beneath the added mobility/clustering/microservice layers.
EdgeCloudSim is a 'CloudSim-based environment' (endpoint description) that reuses CloudSim's engine and adds edge-specific WLAN/WAN network modeling, mobility models and an edge-orchestrator module.

Sibling CloudSim-based edge/fog simulators of the same generation attacking the same modeling gap; EdgeCloudSim emphasizes network/mobility fidelity where iFogSim emphasizes application-placement policies. No precedence between them.
Parallel Python-based fog/IoT simulators built outside the CloudSim/Java lineage: LEAF contributes a granular analytical+DES energy model over application graphs, YAFS a topology/latency focus.

Energy-aware simulators that treat power/energy as the first-class metric: GreenCloud models datacenter server/switch/link power (DVFS/DNS) at packet level, LEAF models fog/edge device energy across thousands of devices.
GreenCloud is 'implemented as an ns-2 extension' (endpoint description), running on the ns-2 packet-level engine that g47 documents; g47 is the corpus's ns-2 reference.
Packet-level datacenter simulators modeling the fabric at packet granularity for different objectives: GreenCloud for energy/DVFS accounting, htsim for transport/congestion-control behavior.

Peer large-scale distributed-system simulators with no precedence: PeerSim targets P2P/overlay protocols (gossip, epidemic, churn) with cycle- and event-driven engines; SimGrid targets distributed applications on grid/cloud/HPC platforms.
Batsim is a 'SimGrid-based ... simulator' (endpoint description): it runs on the SimGrid kernel and layers an RJMS/job-scheduling abstraction (driven by the external batsched scheduler) on top.

BigHouse's Statistical Queuing Simulation instantiates queueing-theoretic datacenter-server models, sampling empirical arrival/service distributions - the applied 'queueing theory in action' method of Harchol-Balter's text.
BigHouse's statistical server-system models are traceable to the classical queueing-theory foundations in Kleinrock Vol. 1.
The survey explicitly catalogs 'iFogSim, EdgeCloudSim, YAFS' as the fog/edge simulation tools it compares and taxonomizes.
Named among the compared tools in the survey's description: 'iFogSim, EdgeCloudSim, YAFS'.
Named among the compared tools in the survey's description: 'iFogSim, EdgeCloudSim, YAFS'.

Parallel surveys of fog/edge simulation tooling with no precedence: g209 emphasizes simulators plus deployment-planners (FogTorchPI/Brogi & Forti), g125 catalogs open-source edge simulators and emulators.

CloudSim is a discrete-event simulator; the DES foundations (event scheduling, random-variate generation, output/statistical analysis) in Banks & Carson are prerequisite to building and trusting CloudSim experiments.

Contemporaneous, independently developed toolkits for simulating distributed/cloud computing: CloudSim models cloud datacenters and VM allocation in Java; SimGrid models distributed applications on grid/cloud/HPC platforms in C.
CloudSim 7G is an integrated extension of the CloudSim core adding 5G/6G and future-network models, refining the original toolkit for next-generation scenarios.
CloudSimSDN builds on CloudSim to model software-defined cloud datacenters, adding dynamic flow routing and bandwidth allocation.
The open-source edge-computing-simulators survey catalogs iFogSim among the fog/edge tools it compares.
The survey catalogs EdgeCloudSim among the edge simulators it compares.
The survey catalogs YAFS among the open-source fog/edge simulators it compares.
The survey catalogs energy-aware fog/edge simulators, including LEAF, among the open-source tools it compares.
RouteNet-Erlang is the Erlang-extended successor in the RouteNet GNN lineage, adding multi-queue scheduling and topology generalization to the original RouteNet model.
RouteNet-Fermi is the later RouteNet-family model, handling non-Markovian traffic and arbitrary scheduling and thereby superseding RouteNet-Erlang's scope.
RouteNet-Gauss is the hardware-enhanced successor to RouteNet-Fermi in the same RouteNet GNN lineage.
The BNN-UPC GNN survey explicitly 'Frames RouteNet-Erlang/Fermi' among its network-modeling use cases.
The BNN-UPC GNN survey explicitly 'Frames RouteNet-Erlang/Fermi' among its network-modeling use cases.
The GNN-for-networks survey catalogs the foundational RouteNet model as the origin of the group's network-modeling line.
The survey covers graph-based deep-learning models built from captured traffic as a GNN network-modeling use case.
The survey covers the GNN-based network digital twin (TwinNet) as a management/optimization use case.
The survey points to the group's GNN datasets and GNNet Challenge infrastructure used to train and benchmark these models.
RouteNet-Erlang, by its own account 'outperforming queueing-theory models,' challenges classical queueing-network/Markov-chain analysis for performance prediction.
RouteNet-Fermi predicts delay/jitter/loss under realistic non-Markovian traffic, challenging the Markov-chain assumptions underlying classical queueing-network models.
RouteNet-Fermi's emphasis on realistic non-Markovian traffic echoes the empirically demonstrated failure of Poisson/Markovian traffic modeling.
m4 is the fully-learned flow-level simulator succeeding m3's hybrid fluid+ML estimator on the same data-center latency task (~100x vs 4-8x speedup).
m3 and MimicNet are sibling ML approaches to fast data-center network performance estimation.
m4 and DeepQueueNet are parallel fully-learned network simulators aimed at scalable, generalized performance estimation.
m4 argues that learned flow-level simulation can replace packet-level DES such as ns-3, which does not scale to large data-center networks.
ns3-gym wraps the ns-3 packet-level simulator as an OpenAI Gym environment, using ns-3 as its underlying simulation engine.
ns3-ai replaces ns3-gym's socket bridge with shared memory, its note reporting '50-100x faster inter-process data exchange than ns3-gym's ZeroMQ.'
ns3-ai bridges the ns-3 simulator to Python AI (DL/RL) frameworks via a shared-memory interface.
NetworkGym and ns3-gym are sibling RL-environment frameworks exposing network simulation to reinforcement-learning agents.
NetworkGym's high-fidelity full-stack RL environments run on the ns-3 simulation backend.
Differentiable DES builds on the discrete-event system simulation paradigm, smoothing its event dynamics to make the simulator differentiable.
Both make network simulation differentiable to enable gradient-based control/optimization — queueing-network control here, traffic engineering there.
Differentiable DES targets control of queueing networks, the objects studied by classical queueing-network theory.
Pantheon (a 'training ground') and ns3-gym (a 'playground') are sibling ML-in-networking training environments: real-path emulation versus RL-in-simulation.
TwinNet builds a network digital twin using the RouteNet GNN as its underlying performance model.
The captured-traffic graph deep-learning model instantiates the RouteNet GNN approach on measured, real traffic.
DeepQueueNet and MimicNet are parallel ML-based network performance estimators targeting scalable data-center/network prediction.
The data-driven digital-twin performance-modeling perspective builds on learned GNN network models such as RouteNet-Fermi as its modeling engine.
Hypatia pairs its satgenpy constellation/routing generator with "an ns-3 packet-level engine" as its simulation core, i.e. it instantiates the ns-3 model library.

StarPerf (analytical constellation-abstraction estimates of area-to-area latency/throughput/coverage) is the analytical sibling to Hypatia's packet-level ns-3 approach; both target the same emerging LEO mega-constellations.

SILLEO-SCNS and StarPerf are both standalone LEO constellation simulators that derive metrics from shortest-path/analytical abstractions (Dijkstra ISL latency) rather than a packet-level engine; parallel analytical tools.
OS3 is a "OMNeT++/INET open-source satellite simulator": it runs on and uses the OMNeT++ discrete-event simulation environment (with INET) as its engine.
Title labels SNS3 an "ns-3 satellite module"; it is literally a module inside the ns-3 model library implementing DVB-S2/RCS2 links.
Both are Magister Solutions system-level satellite/NTN simulators (SNS3: DVB-S2/RCS2 ns-3 module; g226: 5G-NR NTN system simulator) — sibling tools from the same developer group.
StarryNet is a Docker-container emulation framework running real network stacks; it instantiates the container-based network-emulation methodology that g39 establishes for reproducible experiments.

Per the paper, the Magister 5G-NTN system-level simulator is built as a 5G NTN extension of ns-3's 5G-LENA (NR) module, adding 3GPP TR 38.811/38.821 channel and orbital-geometry models — later work in the 5G-LENA lineage.
xeoverse is a "Mininet/VM real-time simulator": it models satellites, terminals and ground stations as lightweight hosts inside Mininet, using the Network-in-a-Laptop prototyping engine.

xeoverse's evaluation benchmarks total simulation time against Hypatia (reported ~2.9x faster), positioning its real-time engine against Hypatia's packet-level simulator on the same mega-constellation workloads.
xeoverse benchmarks against StarryNet (reported ~40x faster) and reports that StarryNet cannot scale to large mega-constellations, empirically comparing the two emulation platforms.
leosatellites is described as the model that "extends OS3 ported to INET 4.3" and validates against FCC-filed constellations — the finer, later work in the OS3 OMNeT++ lineage.
leosatellites is "ported to INET 4.3"; it runs on and uses the INET framework's protocol/model stack as its base.
The LEO satellite networking survey catalogs Hypatia among the LEO simulation platforms used for routing/topology and ISL experimentation.
The survey covers StarPerf as an analytical mega-constellation performance-characterization tool within its treatment of LEO simulation methodology.
The survey catalogs SILLEO-SCNS among standalone LEO constellation simulators for ISL/ground-link design and shortest-path latency.
The survey references StarryNet as a container-based ISTN emulation/digital-twin platform for LEO networking experiments.
The survey catalogs xeoverse as a real-time large-scale LEO mega-constellation simulation platform.
The comprehensive 6G-simulators survey includes the Magister 5G/NR NTN system-level simulator within its NTN simulator scope.
The 6G-simulators survey catalogs Hypatia as a LEO/NTN packet-level simulator relevant to space-terrestrial 6G evaluation.
Title "Comparative Analysis of Three Open-Source 5G Simulation Tools (Simu5G, ...)" — the comparative study empirically benchmarks Simu5G against the other tools.
The three-tool comparative analysis of open-source 5G simulators empirically compares ns-3's 5G-LENA alongside Simu5G.
5G-LENA is the CTTC NR simulator built on and distributed for ns-3 — a component/extension of the ns-3 model ecosystem.
Titled "Simu5G — An OMNeT++ Library for End-to-End Performance Evaluation of 5G"; it is a 5G library within the OMNeT++/INET simulation ecosystem.
Titled "ns-3 mmWave module"; it is an ns-3 module extending the model library with mmWave PHY/MAC (relevant to Ka/mmWave NTN links).

The Anick-Mitra-Sondhi fluid queue (buffer fed by on/off exponential sources, solved by spectral/ODE decomposition) is the foundational fluid-flow model whose coupled-ODE machinery the Misra-Gong-Towsley TCP/AQM fluid model builds on; understand it first.
Gu-Liu-Towsley's hybrid simulation uses the Misra-Gong-Towsley TCP/AQM coupled-ODE fluid model as its fluid component, time-stepping it alongside event-driven packet simulation.
Multilevel-splitting theory derives efficiency conditions and near-optimal splitting factors, giving the rigorous mathematical analysis of the RESTART importance-splitting heuristic.
Heidelberger's classic rare-event survey catalogs the failure-biasing importance-sampling approach for highly dependable Markovian models introduced by this unified framework.
The Juneja-Shahabuddin survey catalogs failure-biasing importance sampling for dependability/reliability models, including this canonical unified Markovian framework.
The survey covers the importance-splitting family, with RESTART as the canonical splitting technique for network buffer-overflow/cell-loss estimation.
The survey covers multilevel splitting and its efficiency analysis among the recent advances in splitting-based rare-event estimation.
Juneja-Shahabuddin (2006) is the later, broader survey extending Heidelberger's 1995 rare-event survey with a decade of advances: multilevel splitting and heavy-tailed importance sampling.
The Rubino-Tuffin edited volume gathers the rare-event Monte Carlo methods, including failure-biasing importance sampling for dependability, into one comprehensive reference.
The Rubino-Tuffin book consolidates the splitting family, with RESTART, within its treatment of rare-event Monte Carlo methods.
The book gathers multilevel-splitting theory among the splitting methods it consolidates for dependability and telecommunications applications.

The Rubino-Tuffin book (2009) and the Juneja-Shahabuddin survey (2006) are the two standard comprehensive references for rare-event simulation, parallel treatments of the same field with no precedence.

The Benaim-Le Boudec mean-field limit derives a deterministic ODE description for N interacting objects, generalizing to interacting populations the fluid/deterministic-limit modeling philosophy pioneered by the Anick-Mitra-Sondhi fluid queue.

Both replace a large stochastic network with a deterministic ODE description: the mean-field interaction limit and the Misra-Gong-Towsley TCP/AQM fluid model are parallel fluid-limit routes to scalable network modeling.

g250 is by its own framing 'part of the movement that established ACM Artifact Review and Badging,' empirically assessing artifact availability/reproducibility across four ACM networking venues against that badging standard.

This artifact/reproducibility survey extends the credibility-of-network-simulation critique (Pawlikowski's credibility work) into the artifact-availability era, quantifying reproducibility empirically.
Baier-Katoen's textbook (transition systems, temporal logics, probabilistic/CTMC model checking) is the foundation to read before PRISM, whose DTMC/CTMC/MDP/PTA verification instantiates that theory.
Understand the probabilistic model-checking foundations (DTMC/CTMC/MDP, LTL/PCTL) taught here before using Storm, a probabilistic model checker built on the same theory.
The transition-system, temporal-logic and reachability foundations in this textbook underpin UPPAAL's timed-automata model checking; read them first.
The LTL/automata-theoretic explicit-state model-checking algorithms SPIN implements are developed in this textbook; read it before the SPIN reference manual.
Statistical model checking presupposes the model-checking problem, temporal logics and (probabilistic) semantics defined in this foundational text.
This applications survey presumes the CTMC/PTA probabilistic model-checking foundations that Principles of Model Checking establishes.
Storm is the modern high-performance successor to PRISM: it consumes PRISM/JANI models but outperforms PRISM on large DTMC/CTMC/MDP instances, replacing it for demanding verification.
PRISM-games 3.0 'Extends the PRISM framework to turn-based and concurrent stochastic multi-player games' with equilibria and time, a finer extension in the PRISM lineage.
The Modest Toolset and Storm are parallel modern quantitative model checkers interoperating through the JANI model-exchange format, with no precedence between them.
UPPAAL-SMC instantiates statistical model checking (simulation plus hypothesis testing), the method g259 surveys, applied to networks of priced/stochastic timed automata.
g256 is 'the statistical model checking engine of UPPAAL' - a component/mode of the UPPAAL tool represented by its tutorial (g253).
SPIN and UPPAAL are the two canonical model checkers for concurrent systems - SPIN for explicit-state untimed PROMELA, UPPAAL for networks of timed automata - parallel workhorses with no precedence.
The survey demonstrates 'probabilistic model checking (via PRISM and probabilistic timed automata)' on real communication protocols, instantiating PRISM's engine.
PRISM's CTMC steady-state/transient verification computes the same Markov-chain performance measures treated analytically in Queueing Networks and Markov Chains; the tools are complementary.
Rare-event simulation targets the buffer-overflow and tail probabilities of the queueing systems whose exact theory is developed in Kleinrock's Queueing Systems, Vol. 1.

Hybrid fluid/packet simulation is motivated by the scalability limits of packet-level Internet simulation articulated in 'Difficulties in Simulating the Internet'; fluid components cut the event load.
Statistical model checking of low-probability (rare) properties must borrow the importance-sampling and splitting techniques surveyed in this rare-event reference to remain statistically efficient.
UPPAAL-SMC integrates importance-splitting (RESTART-style level crossing) to estimate rare/low-probability properties of stochastic timed automata efficiently.
The Modest Toolset's 'modes' simulator is a statistical-model-checking engine, instantiating the SMC method that g259 surveys.

Stochastic network calculus bounds the backlog/buffer-overflow distributions for bursty on/off sources that the Anick-Mitra-Sondhi fluid queue first solved exactly, generalizing that statistical-multiplexing analysis to networks.

gen: Routes swept (live, 2026-07-09): anchor verification + citing works; editor lineage (Obaidat/Boudriga confirmed); network digital twins (dense 2021–2026 harvest incl. ITU-T/IETF standards track); ML/GNN/surrogate simulation (RouteNet family, MimicNet/DeepQueueNet/SplitSim line); 5G/6G simulators (Simu5G, 5G-LENA, Sionna, comparative surveys); cloud/edge simulators (CloudSim lineage + 2025 convergence survey); PADS (Fujimoto 1990→2016→current engines); network calculus & TSN analysis; P4/emulation fidelity; security M&S (cyber ranges, RL agents, datasets). Foundational canon (queueing, DEVS, DES methodology, credibility literature, core simulator papers) is supplied from high-confidence training knowledge and tagged `verified[TRAIN]` — identifiers there should be spot-checked before downstream citation, per the manifest discipline.

Where recall likely thins: (a) hybrid fluid/packet simulation and rare-event simulation for networks (U12 — technique known, consolidated current survey not located); (b) NTN/satellite-specific simulators beyond SatEdgeSim/ISTN mentions (the 6G-simulator survey, item 107, is the best pivot); (c) formal-methods-adjacent modeling (probabilistic model checking of protocols — PRISM/Storm were deliberately not expanded; add if the "systems boundary" fork resolves broad); (d) WSC/MASCOTS per-paper sweep — treated as venue nodes rather than enumerated; (e) commercial tooling (Riverbed, NetSim, EXata) only lightly covered.

What has clearly moved on since the 2015 anchor: simulation tooling (ns-2 → ns-3/OMNeT++-INET ecosystems with dedicated annual venues); an entirely new subfield of network digital twins with ITU-T/IETF standardization; ML-surrogate and differentiable simulation as a credible substitute/accelerator for packet-level DES; GPU-native, ML-integrated wireless simulation (Sionna) displacing MATLAB link-level tools; emulation (container-based, virtual-time-corrected) as a co-equal methodology rather than an afterthought; and reproducibility/artifact norms institutionalized since ~2020. The anchor's Part 2 (performance evaluation) is the most durable — the queueing/NC analytical core is intact, with TSN/deterministic networking as its most active current application. Its Part 4 (simulation methodology) and Part 5 (wireless evaluation) are the most superseded.

Open forks preserved: systems-boundary items (gem5, SST, BookSim, SimGrid, CODES, AstraSim) collected and tagged `other(systems)`/`cloud-datacenter` for later boundary-drawing; anchor chapters not yet decomposed into nodes (two chapters confirmed independently citable via item 2); citation-neighborhood held at 1-hop with 2-hop candidates implicit in the survey-type entries.

Scheduling expansion (2026-07-09 wave, §16). Crawling out from the anchor's DES/queueing core and the MATLAB TrueTime/SimEvents seeds assembled the task/resource-scheduling method spine: networked-control-systems surveys (Hespanha; Zhang/Gao/Kaynak; Gupta/Chow; Zhang/Han/Yu), event/self-triggered control (Tabuada; Heemels/Johansson/Tabuada; Årzén), the real-time schedulability canon (Liu & Layland; Sha et al.; Buttazzo; Baruah/Bertogna/Buttazzo), control/scheduling co-design (Cervin/Eker/Bernhardsson/Årzén feedback scheduling; Eker/Hagander/Årzén; Årzén & Cervin; the weakly-hard survey), compositional worst-case analysis (Real-Time Calculus; SymTA/S), and FMI co-simulation semantics. Every NCS and schedulability identifier here was Crossref-confirmed live this session, so the section is unusually well-grounded for a foundational-canon sweep. Recall thinned on the pre-DOI IFAC event-based-control papers (Årzén 1999, kept verified[TRAIN]; the CDC-2000 co-design introduction and the ECRTS Control Server quarantined at U16–U17 for want of a grounded identifier); probabilistic model-checking of schedulers (PRISM/UPPAAL) was deliberately left as an unexpanded systems-boundary fork.

mat: All six paradigms were swept live. Coverage is strongest and most self-sufficient in two places: (a) the MathWorks-official stratum for wireless system-level simulation — the 2023–2026 stack (wirelessNetworkSimulator core + 5G/WLAN/Bluetooth/Satellite toolboxes + Wireless Network Toolbox packaging) is fully documented by vendor pages, and the key anti-fabrication finding is the packaging migration (File Exchange add-on → in-product/dedicated toolbox), which any downstream citation must respect; and (b) the co-simulation/NCS paradigm, where a mature, independent, peer-reviewed lineage exists (TrueTime → Jitterbug/JitterTime, PiccSIM, NMLab, Simulink↔OPNET, WirelessHART co-sim) — this is the paradigm most relevant to control-over-network problems and is almost entirely non-vendor literature. The academic-simulators paradigm is dominated by one family (Vienna LTE/5G, fully grounded incl. its Springer monograph) plus GTEC and satellite-networking studies that use SatCom Toolbox as the system-of-record. Recall thins in: independent peer-reviewed evaluations of the new (2023+) MathWorks network-simulation stack (the tooling is young; third-party calibration/validation studies against 3GPP/IEEE references were not found this session and may barely exist yet — a genuine gap, not a search failure); the thesis stratum (one unverified representative); and File Exchange beyond the vendor's own add-on. The discrete-event (SimEvents) paradigm shows the inverse profile of §2: vendor documentation is stable and older, while the peer-reviewed record is concentrated in one research lineage (MathWorks + Cassandras/Boston University, WSC/WODES/DEDS 2006–2019) oriented to CPS/ITS rather than classical packet networks — consistent with the framing that MATLAB/Simulink is a minority tool whose network-M&S value is paradigm-specific (hybrid control+network, coexistence, standards-based wireless KPIs, satellite scenarios) rather than general-purpose packet simulation.

Scheduling expansion (2026-07-09 wave, §8). Added the MATLAB/Simulink stack for multi-station task-and-resource scheduling. Two vendor stacks were grounded first-hand: SoC Blockset (Task Manager block — timer/event-driven tasks with period, priority, per-core mapping, preemption, and overrun/drop policy) and SimEvents (the Simulate/Develop-Custom-Scheduler-of-a-Multicore-Control-System examples — tasks as priority-sorted entities on a multi-core server with mutex-protected shared resources, the closest shipped analog to the target capability), plus network-scale MAC schedulers (5G NR round-robin/proportional-fair/best-CQI and a custom nrScheduler; the Stateflow ALOHA/CSMA-CA multinode model). The non-vendor lineage is dominated by the Lund co-design school (TrueTime 2.0 kernel+network co-simulation; the Cervin and Henriksson theses) and the Sant'Anna real-time-task-in-Simulink line (T-Res/tres_bundle, whose citation resolves U3; Brandberg & Di Natale's SimEvents multicore+memory model), with the RTC Toolbox as the MATLAB analytical (worst-case) counterpart and ns3-fmi-export as a concrete Simulink/FMI-to-ns-3 bridge. JitterTime's venue is now pinned (IEEE ETFA 2019, DOI 10.1109/ETFA.2019.8869221; toolbox at github.com/ControlLTH/JitterTime), resolving U5. Recall thinned on File Exchange breadth (only the vendor plus two academic models grounded); Naderlinger's Simulink timing-block papers (WSC/DATE 2017) were index-confirmed but not primary-fetched (kept verified[TRAIN]); the RTC Toolbox's own ETH page presented an expired TLS certificate at access time (tool kept verified[TRAIN]); and independent validation of the young SoC-Blockset/SimEvents scheduler stack against real RTOS traces remains essentially absent — a genuine gap, not a search failure.

verificationLegend.verified-train: high-confidence training-derived knowledge of existence — re-verify identifiers before downstream citation
verificationLegend.unverified: plausible but unconfirmed; quarantined — do not cite downstream without live verification

anchor.label: Anchor map
anchor.semantic: The 2015 anchor volume’s six parts mapped against the corpus routes that expand, supersede, or post-date them — the GEN report’s own organizing scheme.
anchor.question: What happened to each part of the 2015 book — and what exists now that it could not contain?
anchor.computed: Columns are the six anchor parts plus “beyond the anchor” and the meta routes; section cards carry the headers’ own relation phrases; part verdicts quote the coverage summary. Membership only — no inferred relations.

facets.label: Facets
facets.semantic: The tag lattice both reports enforce scope with: subfield/paradigm × type/stratum × recency × section.
facets.question: What exists about X, and how much of it can I actually cite?
facets.computed: Pure filtering over parsed tags; counts computed live. Combines with the global search / verification / corpus filters.

timeline.label: Chronology
timeline.semantic: Publication strata around the 2015 anchor datum; living documentation and tools form their own stratum.
timeline.question: What is pre-anchor canon, what is post-anchor frontier, what is maintained?
timeline.computed: Year parsed from each citation string (c.-years take the first year; ranges take the start); continuous/maintained docs detected as LIVING; unparseable years fall back to the entry’s own recency tag, labelled as such.

matlab.label: MATLAB lens
matlab.semantic: The tool-family intersection corpus: MATLAB/Simulink actually applied to network/system M&S, organized by its six paradigms.
matlab.question: Where is MATLAB/Simulink a real network-M&S vehicle — and where is it a minority tool?
matlab.computed: Paradigm columns with stratum-coded cards; cross-corpus overlaps link into the general corpus; the load-bearing packaging-migration note is carried verbatim.

triage.label: Triage
triage.semantic: The reports’ verification discipline: verified[WEB] vs verified[TRAIN] vs the unverified quarantine, plus coverage self-assessment.
triage.question: What may I cite downstream as-is, what must I re-verify, what is quarantined — and where does recall thin?
triage.computed: Verification split computed from tags; quarantine cards carried verbatim with their “to confirm” notes; coverage summaries quoted whole.

reading.label: Reading graph
reading.semantic: Typed, directed, cyclic-capable reading relations between resources — the twelve-kind vocabulary carried from the SWE corpus (prerequisite-of, refines, subsumes, formalizes, surveys, applies-method-of, companion, evaluates, critiques, supersedes, part-of, references). Every edge is provenance-tagged: derived (grounded in report text) or editorial (maintainer rationale, dotted).
reading.question: What should I read before / after / alongside this resource, and why?
reading.computed: Nodes = every resource with ≥1 typed edge; corpus bands (gen/mat) are shelf-packed to fit the pane; within a band, order is (subfield/paradigm, year). Edges are hued by kind; editorial edges are dotted. Hover traces the cycle-safe closure both directions. The resources with no typed relation remain reachable via Anchor, Facets, Chronology, and search.

graph.label: Overlays
graph.semantic: EDITORIAL typed-relation overlays over a curated subset: a didactic ground-up reading order, and theory→applied transitive-specialization chains. Maintainer judgment, not report fact — every edge carries its rationale.
graph.question: In what order do I read — and how does each theory become a runnable multi-station model?
graph.computed: Levels/stages are hand-assigned in build/overlays.py; within-band order is a pure barycenter pass; acyclicity and level-monotonicity are machine-checked at build time; hover traces the transitive closure along overlay edges.
